summary: Children learn that a fraction requires EQUAL parts — equal in AMOUNT (area), not necessarily equal in shape or appearance. Two load-bearing ideas: having the right NUMBER of pieces is not enough (unequal pieces are not halves/thirds/quarters), and two shares that look completely different can still be equal if they cover the same amount. Teach by partitioning the same shape several ways and by comparing equal-area-but-different-shape pieces, so children judge shares by amount, not by look. Thirds (and a circle into three) force children off repeated halving.
misconceptions: Equal shares must look the same / be congruent — rejects equal-area different-shape pieces as 'not fair'
Any N pieces count as Nths regardless of size (ignores the equal-parts requirement)
A shape can only be partitioned into a fraction one 'proper' way
Judges share size by one dimension (length) rather than area
Thinks halving repeatedly is the only way to make parts, so thirds feel impossible

activities.title: Cut it, re-lay it: equal amount beats equal look
steps: Partition a square into four parts where the pieces look different — e.g. one long thin strip plus some oddly-shaped bits — but each covers the same amount.
Before checking, predict: is the long thin piece the same amount of the square as a fat corner piece? Say why.

Check equality physically: cut the long strip and lay it over the fat piece to see it rearranges exactly onto it. For pieces whose edges follow a faint underlying grid you can also count the unit squares each covers; for diagonal or irregular pieces use cutting and rearrangement rather than counting, since squares get split.
Decide whether all four pieces are quarters and give the reason (each is the same AMOUNT, one of four equal parts).

Now quarter the SAME shape in a completely different way (e.g. three equally spaced vertical cuts giving four equal strips, then a 2x2 grid, then two diagonals) and argue each piece is still a quarter.

Partition a circle into three equal parts (120-degree slices) and explain how you could check the three parts really are equal (overlay one onto another — they are congruent — or compare the area each covers).
activities.insight: A quarter means each part is the same amount (area) of the whole, one of four equal parts — the pieces may look different as long as each covers the same amount; and the same shape can be partitioned into the same fraction in many valid ways.

activities.title: Sort the partitions: quarters or not?
steps: Sort a set of partitioned shapes into 'shows quarters' and 'does not show quarters'.
Include cases that are equal-area but different-shape (these ARE quarters) and cases with four pieces of unequal size (these are NOT quarters).
For each 'does not' card, say what is wrong (pieces are not the same amount).
For each tricky 'is' card where pieces look different, say how you could prove they are equal (cut and rearrange/recompose, or count squares where edges follow the grid).
activities.insight: Whether a partition shows quarters depends on equal amount, not on the number of pieces or on whether the pieces look alike.

activities.title: Which is the bigger share: a third or a quarter?
steps: Take two identical shapes; partition one into three equal parts and the other into four equal parts.
Predict which single piece is bigger: one of three equal parts, or one of four equal parts, of the same shape.

Check by overlaying one piece on the other when both wholes are cut the same way (e.g. both into strips the same direction, or both into slices from the centre of a circle) so the larger covers the smaller and sticks out; otherwise compare the area each covers.
State the reasoning: cutting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller.
activities.insight: For the same whole, one of three equal parts is bigger than one of four equal parts — cutting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller.

checkQuestion: Here is a paper square cut into four parts. The parts look different from each other — one is a long strip, the others are smaller shapes — but they all cover the same amount of the square. Amir says these can't be quarters, because the pieces are different shapes. Is Amir right? Say why or why not. Then show me two DIFFERENT ways to cut this rectangle into four equal parts.
checkAnswer: Amir is wrong — they ARE quarters, because a quarter means each part is the same AMOUNT (area) of the whole, one of four equal parts; the pieces can look different as long as each covers the same amount. For the rectangle, shows two valid quarterings (e.g. three equal vertical cuts, and a 2×2 grid, or two diagonals) and can argue each piece is a quarter.
